name: Winnipeg Art Gallery
features: Da Roza's competition-winning gallery on a triangular site, opened in 1971; Michael Maltzan's Qaumajuq, for Inuit art, joined it in 2021.
why: Suggested by the University of Manitoba art librarian (Winnipeg Building Index), 6 Nov 2026

sources.quote: In 1967, the museum acquired a triangular plot of land across from the Civic Auditorium and launched a competition for architects to submit designs for a new building.
Construction began in 1969, and the new building opened to the public on 25 September 1971.
In 2021, the museum opened a Michael Maltzan-designed Qaumajuq building in order to house the museum's Inuit art collection.

name: Manitoba Legislative Building
by: Frank Worthington Simon, Henry Boddington III
features: Beaux-Arts legislature chosen from 67 competition entries, 77 m tall and crowned by the gilded Golden Boy.
why: Suggested by the University of Manitoba art librarian (Winnipeg Building Index), 6 Nov 2026

sources.quote: The neoclassical, Beaux-Arts-style building was completed in 1920 along with its famed Golden Boy
Standing at 77 metres (253 ft) tall, it was designed and built by Frank Worthington Simon (1862–1933) and Henry Boddington III
Of the 67 submissions, Frank Worthington Simon, a former student at the École des Beaux-Arts, had his design chosen

name: Esplanade Riel
features: Side-spar cable-stayed footbridge over the Red River, with a plaza cantilevered at the base of its tower.

sources.quote: Opened to foot traffic in 2003 and having a grand opening in the summer of 2004, the Esplanade Riel was co-designed by architects Guy Préfontaine and Étienne Gaboury
The bridge includes an architectural composite tower that is prestressed with a cantilevered and stayed semi-circular plaza area at the base of the tower.

name: Precious Blood Church
features: Gaboury's tipi-inspired church, called his most recognizable work by the Winnipeg Architecture Foundation.
why: Suggested by the University of Manitoba art librarian (Winnipeg Building Index), 6 Nov 2026

sources.quote: The church was designed by Canadian architect Étienne Gaboury. Construction of the building was completed in 1968.
The church's tipi-inspired shape has been called Gaboury's most recognizable work by the Winnipeg Architecture Foundation.

name: Union Bank Building, Winnipeg
features: Winnipeg's tallest building when it opened: a steel and concrete frame behind brick and terracotta, on the classical palazzo model.
why: Suggested by the University of Manitoba art librarian (Winnipeg Building Index), 6 Nov 2026

sources.quote: Beginning construction in 1903 and opening in November 1904, the Union Bank Tower was the tallest building in Winnipeg at its completion
Designed by two of Canada’s top architects, Frank Darling and John Andrew Pearson, the Union Bank Tower follows the classical palazzo model
the building was constructed with a network of steel and reinforced concrete that provided support for the brick and terracotta walls.

name: Centennial Concert Hall
by: Green Blankstein Russell, Moody Moore Whenham, Smith Carter Searle
features: A 2,305-seat hall, home of the Winnipeg Symphony Orchestra, the Royal Winnipeg Ballet and Manitoba Opera.
why: Suggested by the University of Manitoba art librarian (Winnipeg Building Index), 6 Nov 2026

sources.quote: The architects of the Hall were Green, Blankstein, Russell Assoc., Moody, Moore, Whenham & Partners, and Smith, Carter, Searle Associates, which are all located in Winnipeg.
The concert hall opened on March 25, 1968.
Centennial Concert Hall is a 2,305-seat performing arts centre

name: Winnipeg Richardson International Airport Terminal
features: A terminal inspired by Winnipeg's landscape and the prairie sky; the first LEED-certified airport terminal in Canada.
commons_category: Category:Winnipeg James Armstrong Richardson International Airport
why: Suggested by the University of Manitoba art librarian (Winnipeg Building Index), 6 Nov 2026

sources.quote: Winnipeg's main airport terminal was designed by Argentine architect Cesar Pelli and Stantec.
construction beginning in 2007 and ending on October 30, 2011, when it was officially opened to the public.
The terminal's design was inspired by the City of Winnipeg's distinctive landscape and Manitoba's vast prairies and sky.
It was the first airport terminal in Canada to be LEED-certified
